content: Diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a synthetic, nonsteroidal estrogen that is orally active. It was first synthesized in 1938. However, in 1971, it was discovered to be a teratogen when administered to pregnant women, meaning it could cause malformations in developing embryos or fetuses. DES was initially synthesized in early 1938 by Leon Goldberg, a graduate student working under Sir Robert Robinson at the Dyson Perrins Laboratory at the University of Oxford. The synthesis was based on a formulation by Wilfrid Lawson at the Courtauld Institute of Biochemistry, led by Sir Edward Charles Dodds at Middlesex Hospital Medical School, University College London. The synthesis was published in Nature on February 5, 1938. Unlike the synthetic steroidal estrogen ethinyl estradiol, which was patented by the German pharmaceutical company Schering, DES was developed by English university researchers funded by the Medical Research Council (MRC), which had a policy against patenting drugs discovered using public funds. As a result, DES was not patented, was inexpensive to produce from coal tar, and was manufactured by over 300 pharmaceutical companies, keeping its price low due to competition. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved DES in tablet form (up to 5 mg) on September 19, 1941, for several indications: gonorrheal vaginitis, atrophic vaginitis, menopausal symptoms, and postpartum lactation suppression to prevent breast engorgement. The indication for gonorrheal vaginitis was later dropped with the advent of penicillin. In 1941, Charles Huggins and Clarence Hodges at the University of Chicago discovered that DES was the first effective drug for treating metastatic prostate cancer. For over 40 years, orchiectomy or DES (or both) were the standard initial treatments for symptomatic advanced prostate cancer until the approval of the gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist leuprolide in 1985, which had similar efficacy but fewer side effects. From the 1940s to the late 1980s, DES was FDA-approved as estrogen-replacement therapy for conditions such as ovarian dysgenesis, premature ovarian failure, and post-oophorectomy states. In the 1940s, it was also prescribed off-label to prevent miscarriages in women with a history of pregnancy loss. On July 1, 1947, the FDA approved the first supplemental new drug application (by Squibb) to include miscarriage prevention as an indication, approving 25 mg and later 100 mg tablets for this purpose. The recommended regimen involved starting at 5 mg per day in the 7th and 8th weeks of pregnancy, with gradual increases to 125 mg per day by the 35th week. DES was initially considered safe and effective for both the pregnant woman and the developing fetus. However, a double-blind study published six years after FDA approval for miscarriage prevention found that DES did not reduce the rates of miscarriage or premature delivery compared to a control group. Despite this, DES continued to be aggressively marketed and prescribed, though its use declined over time. By the late 1960s, most leading obstetrics textbooks stated that DES was ineffective for preventing miscarriage. Between 1941 and 1971, an estimated 5–10 million people in the United States were exposed to DES, including pregnant women and their offspring. In 1960, DES was found to be more effective than androgens in treating advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. It remained the hormonal treatment of choice for this condition for two decades until the approval of tamoxifen in 1977, which had similar efficacy but fewer side effects. DES was also used off-label as a postcoital contraceptive. However, in 1975, the FDA clarified that it had never approved DES for this indication and discouraged its use by removing 25 mg tablets from the market and requiring labeling changes for lower doses to explicitly state that DES should not be used as a postcoital contraceptive. By the 1980s, the Yuzpe regimen of combined oral contraceptive pills replaced DES for emergency contraception. In 1978, the FDA removed postpartum lactation suppression from the approved indications for DES and other estrogens. By the 1990s, the only approved indications for DES were the treatment of advanced prostate cancer and advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women. Eli Lilly, a major manufacturer of DES, ceased production and marketing of the drug in 1997. On April 15, 1971, the New England Journal of Medicine published a report linking DES use during the first trimester of pregnancy to a rare vaginal cancer, clear cell adenocarcinoma (CCA), in female offspring. This led to the FDA advising physicians to stop prescribing DES to pregnant women and to remove miscarriage prevention from its approved indications. DES was confirmed to be a teratogen, but not all exposed individuals experience DES-related health problems. Women prescribed DES during pregnancy have a modestly increased risk of breast cancer, with a fivefold increase after age 40. Female offspring exposed to DES in utero, known as DES Daughters, are at increased risk for CCA of the vagina and cervix, structural abnormalities of the reproductive tract, pregnancy complications, infertility, and autoimmune disorders. DES Daughters are at the highest risk for CCA in their teens and early 20s, though cases have been reported in their 30s and 40s. Male offspring, or DES Sons, may experience feminization, cryptorchidism (undescended testes), or hypospadias (a congenital condition affecting the urethra). A 2002 study suggested a 20-fold increase in hypospadias prevalence among DES Sons, though follow-up research indicated a lower risk. Current research is investigating the third generation of DES exposure, referring to the grandchildren of women who took DES during pregnancy. While data is limited, potential effects include preterm labor, premature birth, and associated complications such as cerebral palsy, blindness, or neurological deficits. A 2003 study suggested that DES exposure might have transgenerational effects, as evidenced by a rare tumor in a 15-year-old girl whose maternal grandmother had taken DES during pregnancy. In veterinary medicine, DES has been successfully used to treat female canine incontinence caused by poor sphincter control. At low doses (1 mg), it does not exhibit the carcinogenic properties seen in humans. It is typically administered daily for five days, followed by maintenance dosing every 4–7 days as needed.
